title: The Teacher's First Test of the Day, Part 1
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart opens with a passage from Jocko Willink's Extreme Ownership, in which the former Navy SEAL frames the moment an alarm clock goes off as the day's "first test": getting up shows discipline, hitting snooze shows weakness, and the pattern set in that decisive moment ripples into bigger decisions later in the day. Stuart acknowledges that Willink's intensity, framing tiredness as "weakness" and "failure," doesn't match his usual tone on the blog, but defends including it using the aphorism that "hard words make soft people, and soft words make hard people," arguing that a bracing outside perspective is sometimes valuable. He admits candidly that he's personally been failing this test lately, waking to his 5:00 or 5:30 alarm only about half the time over the past two weeks, but notes that on the days he does get up, he notices a real difference in his thinking, writing, teaching, and overall enjoyment of the day. The piece ends by teeing up a sequel: what is the equivalent "first test" for a class period, rather than a day?
points: Stuart imports Jocko Willink's alarm-clock framing directly, treating the moment of waking as a discipline test whose outcome "translates to more significant decisions" throughout the day.

He deliberately flags the tonal mismatch between Willink's harsh SEAL-instructor framing and his own usual voice, using it as an occasion to explain why he still finds value in blunter outside perspectives.

His personal admission of failing the test roughly half the time recently models the vulnerability-plus-practical-payoff pattern common in his writing: he doesn't just cite the idea, he reports what happens on the days he actually follows it.
The piece is explicitly structured as part one of a pair, ending on an open question (what's the first test of a class period?) that sets up the follow-up post on start-of-class procedures.
quotes: The moment the alarm goes off is the first test; it sets the tone for the rest of the day. The test is not a complex one: when the alarm goes off, do you get up out of bed, or do you lie there in comfort and fall back to sleep?
If you have the discipline to get out of bed, you win — you pass the test. If you are mentally weak for that moment and you let that weakness keep you in bed, you fail.

But a friend once gave me this aphorism to chew on: hard words make soft people, and soft words make hard people. And I think we need folks like Willink once in a while to speak a radically different perspective into our lives.
Lately, I've mostly not passed this test. Of the past ten weekdays, I'd guess I've woken up at my 5:00 or 5:30 am alarm clock maybe half of the days.
BUT each of the times I've done it, I really do notice a difference in my thinking, my writing, my teaching, and my general enjoyment of the day.
